stem: Partition created Pakistan in 1947. What was its most immediate human consequence?
options: (A) Immediate peaceful prosperity in both new states
(B) Reunification of India and Pakistan within a decade under a single government
(C) Mass communal violence and the displacement of some 15 million people
(D) British troops remaining to keep order
explanation: Drawing the border between India and Pakistan uprooted some 15 million people and unleashed communal slaughter in which hundreds of thousands died — the largest mass migration in human history and one of its bloodiest partitions. (A) is wrong because partition brought violence and chaos, not immediate prosperity. (B) is wrong because India and Pakistan did not reunify; they fought wars instead. (D) is wrong because British troops withdrew rapidly; no British force stayed to keep order.

stem: In 1990-91, republic after republic declared sovereignty and the Soviet Union dissolved. Why did resurgent nationalism prove fatal to the USSR?
stimulus: A timeline of 1988-1991 shows a cascade of sovereignty declarations: Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, then Ukraine, Belarus, the Central Asian republics, and others — each asserting independence from Moscow in rapid succession.
options: (A) The USSR was ethnically homogeneous
(B) Nationalism strengthened Moscow's central control
(C) The republics demanded tighter centralization
(D) Glasnost uncorked suppressed national movements
explanation: The USSR was an empire of over a hundred nationalities held together by force and ideology. Once glasnost loosened censorship and permitted open debate, Estonians, Latvians, Lithuanians, Ukrainians, and others revived long-buried independence movements that Moscow could no longer suppress — and the union dissolved republic by republic. (A) is wrong because the USSR was among the most ethnically diverse states on earth. (B) is wrong because nationalism pulled the republics outward, away from Moscow's control. (C) is wrong because the republics demanded sovereignty and separation, not tighter centralization.

stem: Why did Gorbachev's policies of glasnost and perestroika fail to save the Soviet Union?
options: (A) They abolished the Communist Party's leading role in 1986
(B) Unleashed criticism and half-measures that wrecked the planned economy
(C) They returned the USSR to full Stalinist central planning and censorship
(D) They severed all Soviet trade with Eastern Europe
explanation: Glasnost freed criticism that exposed and delegitimized the Party, while perestroika's partial reforms disrupted the planned economy without building a functioning market — the combination unraveled the system Gorbachev meant to rescue. (A) is wrong because the Party's monopoly was not abolished in 1986; Gorbachev worked through it. (C) is wrong because the reforms moved away from, not back to, Stalinist control. (D) is wrong because Soviet-Eastern European trade continued during the reforms.

stem: Why did the 1986 Chernobyl disaster damage the Soviet government's legitimacy?
options: (A) It physically destroyed Moscow
(B) The cover-up exposed lying and incompetence
(C) It was revealed as American sabotage
(D) It proved nuclear power was entirely safe
explanation: Moscow first tried to hide the explosion, delaying evacuation and denying the severity — but radiation monitors in Sweden made the cover-up impossible. The lying exposed the system's instinct for secrecy and incompetence, discrediting official claims and feeding the glasnost-era demand for truthfulness. (A) is wrong because Chernobyl is in Ukraine, far from Moscow, which was never destroyed. (C) is wrong because there is no evidence of American sabotage; the cause was flawed reactor design and operator error. (D) is wrong because the disaster horrified the world about nuclear risks; it proved nothing about safety.

stem: Which of the following best contrasts the origins of Japan's 1990s stagnation and Russia's 1990s economic collapse?
options: (A) Japan suffered hyperinflation while Russia's prices stayed stable
(B) Both economies were wrecked by ethnic conflict
(C) Both crises were fundamentally foreign-debt crises
(D) A burst asset bubble in Japan; dismantled planning in Russia
explanation: The two crises had different origins: Japan's lost decade began when its 1980s asset bubble burst in 1990-91, leaving banks holding bad loans inside an intact market economy, while Russia's GDP fell by roughly half as shock therapy dismantled central planning. (A) is wrong because Japan experienced deflation, not hyperinflation, and Russia's prices exploded. (B) is wrong because ethnic conflict drove neither crisis. (C) is wrong because neither crisis was fundamentally a foreign-debt crisis.

stem: The US and USSR cooperated against Japan in 1945 while American officers were already maneuvering to limit Soviet gains in Korea. What does this reveal about their relationship?
stimulus: Paraphrase of a US Army account of 1945: American planners needed a surrender line in Korea as far north as the Soviets would accept, knowing Russian troops could overrun the entire peninsula before US forces arrived from Okinawa, 600 miles away. The task was to craft an arrangement the Soviets would accept while preventing them from seizing all of Korea.
options: (A) An alliance of convenience already fraying with mutual suspicion
(B) Open enemies already at war
(C) Close and trusting friends
(D) Powers with no contact at all
explanation: Washington and Moscow fought Japan together in 1945, yet Bonesteel's account shows American officers already scheming to limit Soviet gains in Korea. The alliance was a temporary convergence against a common enemy, with mutual suspicion shaping every joint decision even before the war ended.

stem: The 38th parallel was meant as a temporary surrender line. Why did it become a permanent border?
stimulus: Paraphrase of a US Army account of 1945: American planners needed a surrender line in Korea as far north as the Soviets would accept, knowing Russian troops could overrun the entire peninsula before US forces arrived from Okinawa, 600 miles away. The task was to craft an arrangement the Soviets would accept while preventing them from seizing all of Korea.
options: (A) Koreans voted for division
(B) Japan redrew the border in 1950 during the outbreak of the Korean War to aid the South
(C) China imposed the division
(D) Each superpower built a rival regime in its zone and neither would yield
explanation: Washington built the Republic of Korea in the south and Moscow built the Democratic People's Republic in the north, each claiming all of Korea. Neither patron would sacrifice its client, so the 'temporary' line froze into a permanent frontier, then a war, then a standoff that endures today.

stem: The US drew a line in Korea partly to limit how much territory the Soviets would occupy. Which later doctrine formalized this approach?
stimulus: Paraphrase of a US Army account of 1945: American planners needed a surrender line in Korea as far north as the Soviets would accept, knowing Russian troops could overrun the entire peninsula before US forces arrived from Okinawa, 600 miles away. The task was to craft an arrangement the Soviets would accept while preventing them from seizing all of Korea.
options: (A) Detente
(B) Rollback
(C) Containment
(D) Isolationism
explanation: Containment, articulated by George Kennan, held that Soviet expansion must be blocked wherever it threatened, through alliances, aid, and force, without attempting to roll back communism where it already ruled. Drawing a line in Korea was containment in embryo.

stem: Brutus writes that Sharpeville's importance is not that seventy died, but that it 'epitomized oppression.' Why does he insist the massacre revealed rather than created the reality?
stimulus: Paraphrase of Dennis Brutus's 1973 poem on Sharpeville (1960): Black South Africans gathered unarmed before police stations to protest the pass laws, and at Sharpeville police fired into the crowd. What matters, the poet says, is not the seventy dead, nor even that they were shot in the back while fleeing, but that the day laid bare the nature of the society: racial dominance defined, the will to oppress demonstrated. What the world whispers, apartheid declares with guns.
options: (A) The massacre exposed apartheid's constant violence rather than creating it
(B) Sharpeville was a peaceful protest
(C) The world already fully understood apartheid
(D) Apartheid was a mild and tolerant system before Sharpeville radicalized the government
explanation: Brutus insists Sharpeville's importance is not the body count but what it exposed: the massacre made visible the daily, grinding violence of apartheid that the world preferred not to see. The bullets merely announced what the system was.

stem: The Sharpeville protesters were demonstrating against the pass laws. What did the pass laws do?
stimulus: Paraphrase of Dennis Brutus's 1973 poem on Sharpeville (1960): Black South Africans gathered unarmed before police stations to protest the pass laws, and at Sharpeville police fired into the crowd. options: (A) They gave Black South Africans the vote
(B) They freed political prisoners
(C) They controlled Black South Africans' movement, residence, and work
(D) They applied to white citizens
explanation: Under apartheid, Black South Africans had to carry passbooks documenting identity and residence, and could be arrested for being in the wrong place. The Sharpeville crowd gathered precisely to defy that system of movement control, the daily machinery of racial domination.

stem: In 1994 South Africa held its first election open to all races, and Nelson Mandela became president. Why was this a world-historical event?
stimulus: Paraphrase of Dennis Brutus's 1973 poem on Sharpeville (1960): Black South Africans gathered unarmed before police stations to protest the pass laws, and at Sharpeville police fired into the crowd. What matters, the poet says, is not the seventy dead, nor even that they were shot in the back while fleeing, but that the day laid bare the nature of the society: racial dominance defined, the will to oppress demonstrated. What the world whispers, apartheid declares with guns.
options: (A) It established apartheid
(B) Mandela lost the election
(C) White South Africans boycotted the vote, refusing to accept majority rule
(D) It peacefully ended white minority rule through the ballot box
explanation: For the first time, South Africa's Black majority, 27 years after Sharpeville and after decades of struggle, chose its own government. Mandela's victory proved that entrenched white minority rule could be dismantled at the ballot box rather than only on the battlefield.

stem: Gorbachev called for perestroika, 'restructuring.' What was he trying to restructure?
stimulus: Paraphrase of Mikhail Gorbachev's speeches to the Communist Party congress (1985): The Soviet Union will expand cooperation with socialist states and supports peoples struggling against colonial oppression; Asia, Africa, and Latin America are our friends in the fight for peace. But the United States pursues a gigantic space weapons program and builds ever newer arms, hoping its technological edge will defeat socialism through war or blackmail. Only democratization can build a healthy, dynamic economy: radical reform must blend planning with the market, harmonize forms of socialist ownership, and free producers' initiative. A new farm policy will dismantle administrative command in agriculture, restoring the peasant's control over land, machinery, and produce.
options: (A) The bloated Soviet army, its command structure, and military doctrine
(B) The Russian alphabet
(C) Nothing at all
(D) The rigid centrally planned economy, through market mechanisms
explanation: Perestroika meant rebuilding the Soviet economic machine: state enterprises would get initiative, private plots and cooperatives would be legalized, and plan targets would bend to market signals. Gorbachev hoped to save socialism by grafting market incentives onto it.

stem: Reagan's military buildup in the 1980s pressured the Soviet economy. Why couldn't the USSR keep up?

options: (A) The USSR had no army to fund
(B) The United States disarmed in the 1980s
(C) Its inefficient planned economy could not match US defense spending
(D) The Soviet economy was larger than America's and far more productive in every sector
explanation: The American economy, roughly twice the Soviet Union's size and far more innovative, could absorb massive defense spending; the Soviet planned economy could not. Every ruble for missiles was a ruble stolen from farms and factories, and the strain helped break the system.

(B) It made Gorbachev stronger
(C) It had no historical significance and changed nothing in Soviet politics at all
(D) Its failure destroyed the Party's authority and doomed the Union
explanation: The hardliners seized Gorbachev to stop the union's dissolution, but Boris Yeltsin defied them from atop a tank, and the army refused to fire. The coup collapsed in three days, destroying the Communist Party's authority and leaving Yeltsin's Russia as the real power; the USSR formally dissolved four months later.

stem: China liberalized its economy but kept one-party rule; the USSR liberalized politics and collapsed. What lesson did Beijing draw?
stimulus: Paraphrase of Mikhail Gorbachev's speeches to the Communist Party congress (1985): The Soviet Union will expand cooperation with socialist states and supports peoples struggling against colonial oppression; Asia, Africa, and Latin America are our friends in the fight for peace. Only democratization can build a healthy, dynamic economy: radical reform must blend planning with the market, harmonize forms of socialist ownership, and free producers' initiative. options: (A) China copied Gorbachev's political reforms and opened the system to multiparty elections
(B) China abandoned all reform
(C) The Soviet Union succeeded
(D) Market reform was safe but political reform fatal, so the Party kept politics closed
explanation: Beijing watched Moscow's experiment and drew the opposite conclusion: Deng's market reforms had delivered growth, while Gorbachev's political opening delivered collapse. The Party's lesson, enforced at Tiananmen in 1989, was that economic liberalization must never be paired with political liberalization.

stem: UN Resolution 181 (1947) proposed the partition of Palestine. What happened to the plan?
stimulus: Paraphrase of UN Resolution 181 (II) on the future government of Palestine (1947): The General Assembly, acting on its special committee's report, finds that Palestine's situation threatens friendly relations among nations. It recommends that Britain, as the mandatory power, and all UN members adopt the Plan of Partition with Economic Union: independent Arab and Jewish states, with a special international regime for Jerusalem, to come into being after the British evacuation, no later than October 1948.
options: (A) Both sides accepted it peacefully and implemented the partition without conflict
(B) The UN imposed it by force
(C) It proposed Arab and Jewish states; Arab rejection led to war
(D) It was never actually proposed
explanation: The resolution proposed ending the British mandate and creating independent Arab and Jewish states with an economic union, Jerusalem under international control. Jewish leaders accepted; Arab leaders rejected partition outright, and civil war began even before Israel declared independence in May 1948.

stem: Which development most directly challenged the Washington Consensus in the late 1990s?
options: (A) The collapse of the Soviet Union
(B) The founding of the WTO in 1995
(C) The East Asian financial crisis of 1997
(D) The adoption of the euro as Europe's common currency
explanation: The 1997 East Asian crisis shook faith in the Consensus: critics argued that the rapid capital-market liberalization it prescribed had made developing economies vulnerable to sudden outflows, and the IMF's austerity prescriptions deepened the recessions. (A) is wrong because the Soviet collapse initially seemed to vindicate market reform, not challenge it. (B) is wrong because the WTO embodied the Consensus's open-trade agenda. (D) is wrong because the euro was a European integration project, not a verdict on development policy.

stem: One economist claims that spreading markets is an effective strategy for encouraging democracy. Which case most challenges the claim that market reform leads to political liberalization?
stimulus: One economist argues that an effective strategy for encouraging democracy is the spread of markets. Another adds that globalization and free trade spur economic growth and bring lower prices on many goods.
options: (A) South Korea after 1960
(B) Taiwan after 1970
(C) Eastern Europe after 1989
(D) China after 1978
explanation: Since 1978 China has built one of the world's great market economies while the Communist Party has tightened, not loosened, political control — most visibly in 1989 and after. Marketization without democratization directly contradicts the claim that economic freedom produces political freedom. (A) is wrong because South Korea's market economy did accompany a transition to democracy. (B) is wrong because Taiwan similarly democratized as it grew. (C) is wrong because Eastern Europe's market transitions followed the collapse of one-party rule.

stem: Both speakers praise free trade and open markets. Which policy would both most likely support?
stimulus: One economist argues that an effective strategy for encouraging democracy is the spread of markets. Another adds that globalization and free trade spur economic growth and bring lower prices on many goods.
options: (A) Nationalizing oil industries
(B) Reducing tariffs between nations
(C) Imposing strict import quotas
(D) Fixing prices by government decree
explanation: Both speakers celebrate open markets and competition; lowering tariffs is the signature policy of that creed, expanding trade and lowering consumer prices. (A) is wrong because nationalizing oil industries replaces markets with state control. (C) is wrong because strict import quotas restrict the free trade both speakers praise. (D) is wrong because government price-fixing violates the market mechanism at the heart of their argument.

stem: Image B is a photograph showing a boy and an elderly woman sharing a laptop in front of a rural house in Myanmar. What does this image best illustrate?
stimulus: Image A: children sitting together outdoors, each absorbed in a smartphone, not speaking to one another. Image B: a boy and an elderly woman sharing a laptop in front of a typical rural house in Myanmar.
options: (A) Technology is destroying indigenous cultures
(B) Only young people can learn to use computers
(C) Digital technology reaching the developing world
(D) Laptops in developing countries are used only for business
explanation: The image places a laptop — the emblem of the digital age — in the hands of a child and an elderly woman outside a rural house in Myanmar, a developing country. It shows digital technology reaching far beyond wealthy cities into the developing world. (A) is wrong because the image celebrates access, not cultural destruction; no indigenous practice is shown being harmed. (B) is wrong because the elderly woman shares the laptop, disproving any young-only claim. (D) is wrong because nothing in the image indicates the laptop is used for business.

stem: Image A shows children sitting together outdoors, each absorbed in a smartphone and not speaking to one another. What social concern does the image raise?
stimulus: Image A: children sitting together outdoors, each absorbed in a smartphone, not speaking to one another. Image B: a boy and an elderly woman sharing a laptop in front of a typical rural house in Myanmar.
options: (A) Devices can isolate people sharing a space
(B) Smartphones are now cheap enough for every child
(C) Technology encourages children to enjoy the outdoors
(D) Technology has no effect on social life
explanation: The children share physical space but inhabit separate digital worlds — together yet alone. The image warns that devices can erode face-to-face interaction even among people sitting side by side. (B) is wrong because the image says nothing about what the phones cost. (C) is wrong because the children are ignoring the outdoors, not enjoying it. (D) is wrong because the entire point of the image is technology's visible social effect.

stem: Early home internet connections ran over telephone lines built for voice calls. What problem did the modem solve?
stimulus: Image A: children sitting together outdoors, each absorbed in a smartphone, not speaking to one another. Image B: a boy and an elderly woman sharing a laptop in front of a typical rural house in Myanmar.
options: (A) It translated digital data into audio signals and back again
(B) It increased the speed of light through copper wire to accelerate transmission
(C) It replaced the need for a home computer
(D) It transmitted television signals into homes
explanation: Phone networks were built to carry the human voice as audio, not computer data as bits. The modem bridged that gap by modulating digital data into sound for transmission and demodulating it back at the other end — which is why early connections literally sang and screeched. (B) is wrong because the modem did not change the speed of light or the physical limits of wires. (C) is wrong because the modem connected computers to phone lines; it did not replace computers. (D) is wrong because television signals traveled by broadcast and cable, a separate technology.

stem: Which statement about the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) is most accurate?
options: (A) It established a binding world court with enforcement powers
(B) It applied only to the Allied powers
(C) It was rejected by the General Assembly
(D) Eleanor Roosevelt chaired its drafting committee
explanation: Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the UN Commission on Human Rights, the body that drafted the Declaration in 1946-48. (A) is wrong because the UDHR is a non-binding declaration; it created no court and no enforcement powers. (B) is wrong because its rights are declared universal, applying to all people. (C) is wrong because the General Assembly adopted it 48-0, with eight abstentions.

stem: Roosevelt's phrase 'small places, close to home' referred to which of the following?
options: (A) Neighborhoods, schools, and workplaces of daily life
(B) The courtrooms of international tribunals at The Hague
(C) The chambers of the UN Security Council
(D) Remote regions beyond the reach of any government
explanation: In her 1958 remarks on the Declaration's tenth anniversary, Roosevelt located human rights in 'small places, close to home' — the neighborhood, the school, the factory, farm, or office where every person lives daily life. (B) is wrong because she contrasted lived daily practice with distant institutions like courts. (C) is wrong because the Security Council is the opposite of a 'small place.' (D) is wrong because she meant the places where people actually live, not places beyond government.

stem: Many newly independent nations after 1945 wrote bills of rights into their constitutions. What influence did the UDHR exert on them?
stimulus: Paraphrase of Eleanor Roosevelt's 1958 remarks on human rights, delivered on the tenth anniversary of the Universal Declaration: Where do universal rights begin? In small places, close to home — places so small and so close that they cannot be seen on any maps of the world. Yet they are the world of the individual person: the neighborhood he lives in, the school or college he attends, the factory, farm, or office where he works. These are the places where every man, woman, and child seeks equal justice, equal opportunity, and equal dignity without discrimination. Unless these rights have meaning there, they have little meaning anywhere. Without concerted citizen action to uphold them close to home, we shall look in vain for progress in the larger world. The Declaration itself, adopted in 1948, opens by recalling that disregard for human rights produced barbarous acts that outraged the conscience of mankind, and proclaims a common standard of achievement for all peoples and nations.
options: (A) It was a binding treaty that compelled all states to obey it
(B) Newly independent states universally rejected its principles
(C) It applied only to European nations
(D) A model vocabulary of rights that new states adopted
explanation: Though not legally binding, the UDHR supplied a ready-made vocabulary of universal rights — equality, dignity, non-discrimination — that new states wove into constitutions to signal modernity and win international legitimacy. (A) is wrong because the UDHR was a declaration, not a binding treaty; states could not be compelled by it. (B) is wrong because many new states eagerly adopted rights language rather than rejecting it. (C) is wrong because the Declaration proclaimed itself a 'common standard of achievement for all peoples and all nations,' not a Europe-only document.

stem: Latin American Liberation Theology of the 1960s-70s organized 'base communities' where the poor studied scripture together and took social action. What was the movement's central claim?
stimulus: Paraphrase of Eleanor Roosevelt's 1958 remarks on human rights, delivered on the tenth anniversary of the Universal Declaration: Where do universal rights begin? In small places, close to home — places so small and so close that they cannot be seen on any maps of the world. The Declaration itself, adopted in 1948, opens by recalling that disregard for human rights produced barbarous acts that outraged the conscience of mankind, and proclaims a common standard of achievement for all peoples and nations.
options: (A) The Church should withdraw entirely from politics
(B) Poverty is God's will and should not be challenged
(C) Active struggle for social justice for the poor
(D) Theology should concern itself only with the afterlife
explanation: Liberation theologians such as Gustavo Gutierrez argued that God takes the side of the poor, so the Church must move beyond charity to active struggle against the structures — military regimes, latifundia, foreign exploitation — that produced poverty. Base communities put that into practice through collective Bible study tied to social action. (A) is wrong because the movement sought justice through organized popular action, not withdrawal from politics. (B) is wrong because it treated poverty as an injustice to be fought, not a divine decree. (D) is wrong because its focus was squarely on transforming this world, not only on salvation in the next.

stem: Postwar Western European welfare states differed from the Soviet model most fundamentally in which way?
options: (A) Market economies with broad social protections
(B) They abolished all private property
(C) They rejected any state role in the economy
(D) They provided no pensions or health coverage
explanation: Western Europe built welfare states on top of market economies — private enterprise plus pensions, health care, and unemployment insurance — while the USSR ran a command economy with state ownership of nearly everything. (B) is wrong because Western Europe kept private property; abolishing it was the Soviet approach. (C) is wrong because welfare states expanded the state's economic role. (D) is wrong because pensions and health coverage were the welfare state's signature achievements.

stem: Under international law, why does the distinction between 'migrant' and 'refugee' matter?
stimulus: They keep coming — farmhands and bricklayers, nannies and teachers, programmers and laborers — millions of people leaving home each year for work, higher pay, or simply a better life. Roughly 190 million people now live outside their country of birth, and two to three million more join them annually. Among them are some ten million refugees, driven out by war, famine, or persecution. Bangladeshi workers fly to Malaysian construction sites; West Africans crowd boats bound for Europe; Mexicans cross the northern border for American jobs. Though migrants are a small share of humanity, their movement reshapes the economies and politics of both the lands they leave and the lands they enter.
options: (A) Refugees are always more numerous than migrants
(B) Migrants can never become citizens of their new country
(C) The two terms are legally identical
(D) Refugees cannot be forcibly returned; migrants can
explanation: The legal distinction turns on compulsion: refugees are defined by forced flight from persecution, war, or disaster, and international law — above all the 1951 Refugee Convention's principle of non-refoulement — forbids returning them to danger. Economic migrants, however sympathetic, enjoy no such treaty protection. (A) is wrong because numbers vary by crisis; the legal line is about cause, not headcount. (B) is wrong because migrants can and do naturalize in receiving countries. (C) is wrong because the terms carry very different legal consequences.

stem: By the 2020s, migrants were sending home over $800 billion a year in remittances. What does this reveal about migration's economic impact?

Roughly 190 million people now live outside their country of birth, and two to three million more join them annually. Among them are some ten million refugees, driven out by war, famine, or persecution. Bangladeshi workers fly to Malaysian construction sites; West Africans crowd boats bound for Europe; Mexicans cross the northern border for American jobs. Though migrants are a small share of humanity, their movement reshapes the economies and politics of both the lands they leave and the lands they enter.
options: (A) Remittances are paid only to governments
(B) Migrants as major economic actors for home countries
(C) Migration has no measurable economic effects
(D) Remittances flow from poor countries to rich ones
explanation: Remittances — money migrants send to families back home — grew into one of the largest financial flows to the developing world, often exceeding foreign aid and investment. They pay for food, schooling, and housing, making migrants pivotal economic actors for their countries of origin. (A) is wrong because remittances go overwhelmingly to families, not governments. (C) is wrong because the sums involved demonstrably transform household economies. (D) is wrong because the flow runs from richer receiving countries to poorer home countries, not the reverse.

stem: In the early 1900s, millions migrated from Europe to the Americas. By the late 1900s, the dominant direction had reversed. What best explains the reversal?
stimulus: They keep coming — farmhands and bricklayers, nannies and teachers, programmers and laborers — millions of people leaving home each year for work, higher pay, or simply a better life. Roughly 190 million people now live outside their country of birth, and two to three million more join them annually. Among them are some ten million refugees, driven out by war, famine, or persecution. Bangladeshi workers fly to Malaysian construction sites; West Africans crowd boats bound for Europe; Mexicans cross the northern border for American jobs. Though migrants are a small share of humanity, their movement reshapes the economies and politics of both the lands they leave and the lands they enter.
options: (A) Europe became the destination; developing regions the source
(B) The United States banned all European immigration
(C) Europe's population disappeared entirely
(D) Developing nations grew richer than Europe and attracted its workers
explanation: A century ago Europe was poor and crowded, pushing emigrants outward; by the late twentieth century it had grown wealthy and its birthrates had fallen, turning it into a magnet for immigrants. Meanwhile, population growth and limited opportunity in developing regions supplied the emigrants. The push and pull reversed sides. (B) is wrong because the United States never banned all European immigration. (C) is wrong because Europe's population did not vanish; it stabilized. (D) is wrong because developing regions remained poorer on average; the gap is precisely what drives the flow.

stem: Sociologists call the spread of identical standardized business models worldwide 'McDonaldization.' What does a McDonald's in Shenzhen, China, illustrate?
stimulus: The illustration shows a McDonald's restaurant, golden arches and all, operating in Shenzhen, China.
options: (A) The global diffusion of standardized American consumer culture
(B) China's total rejection of Western culture in favor of traditional local cuisine
(C) American corporate poverty relief
(D) The triumph of communism
explanation: A McDonald's in Shenzhen, identical in menu and golden arches to one in Ohio, shows consumer culture standardized across civilizations. The same brands, the same tastes, the same built environment: globalization made visible in a single restaurant.

stem: When pandemic lockdowns closed factories in Shenzhen, car plants in Germany idled for lack of parts. What does this show?
stimulus: The illustration shows a McDonald's restaurant, golden arches and all, operating in Shenzhen, China.
options: (A) Global supply chains make national economies interdependent
(B) Nations are economically self-sufficient and immune to foreign disruptions
(C) Only China matters in world trade
(D) International trade has ended
explanation: Modern manufacturing strings components across continents: a German car contains Chinese electronics, Mexican wiring, and Korean steel. When one link breaks, the whole chain stalls, so a lockdown in Shenzhen idles factories in Bavaria. Interdependence is the price of efficiency.

stem: 'Engagement' theory held that trading with authoritarian states would liberalize them. Which event contradicts this?

stem: The chart shows life expectancy rising worldwide but lowest in sub-Saharan Africa. What best explains the gap?
stimulus: The chart plots life expectancy by region from 1950 to 2020: a steady global rise, with Western Europe, Canada, and Australia highest, Asia in the middle, and sub-Saharan Africa lowest, though rising.
options: (A) Poverty-related disease burden and weaker health systems
(B) Genetic differences between populations explain the entire gap
(C) Climate alone
(D) Africans do not age
explanation: The chart shows global life expectancy climbing, but sub-Saharan Africa trailing far behind. The gap reflects disease burden: malaria, tuberculosis, HIV/AIDS, and weak health systems, the epidemiological profile of poverty, not of genes or climate alone.

stem: As life expectancy rises in wealthy countries, rates of heart disease and Alzheimer's increase. Why?

(C) Old people are inherently unhealthy

explanation: When sanitation, vaccines, and antibiotics let most people survive childhood and middle age, populations live long enough for chronic diseases of aging to appear. Rising Alzheimer's and heart disease rates are, paradoxically, evidence of public-health success.

stem: Malaria kills hundreds of thousands yearly, mostly in Africa. Why has it persisted there?
stimulus: The chart plots life expectancy by region from 1950 to 2020: a steady global rise, with Western Europe, Canada, and Australia highest, Asia in the middle, and sub-Saharan Africa lowest, though rising.
options: (A) Malaria is a new disease
(B) Tropical mosquito ecology combined with poverty-limited prevention
(C) Africans are naturally immune to malaria after centuries of exposure to the parasite
(D) Cold weather spreads malaria
explanation: Warm, wet tropical climates breed the Anopheles mosquitoes that carry malaria, and poverty means too few bed nets, too little drainage, and too little medicine. The disease persists where ecology favors the mosquito and economics deny the defenses.

stem: The development described in the passage best fits which of the following broader historical contexts?
stimulus: Under the Song dynasty (960-1279), the imperial examinations tested candidates on the Confucian classics. Thousands of scholars competed each year, and those who passed became salaried officials of a centralized state. Study of Confucian texts became the recognized path to government office, and the emperor presented himself as the guardian of Confucian moral order.
options: (A) The Song created the world's first merit-based government by inventing the civil service examination system, which had no precedent in any earlier Chinese dynasty.
(B) The Song continued and expanded the Chinese imperial tradition of ruling through a trained, Confucian-educated bureaucracy.
(C) The Song rejected Confucianism and reorganized the state around Buddhist monasteries.
(D) The examinations gave poor peasant families the same access to high office as wealthy ones.
explanation: Civil service examinations began under earlier dynasties, and the Song expanded them into the main route to office. This continued China's long pattern of legitimating imperial rule through Confucian learning and a professional bureaucracy — a continuity, not an invention.

stem: The Aztec tribute system described in the passage best fits which of the following broader historical patterns?
stimulus: The Codex Mendoza, an Aztec record book, lists the tribute owed by conquered provinces: bales of cotton, loads of maize and beans, cacao beans, warriors' costumes, and feathers. Royal officials called calpixque collected these goods each year and delivered them to the capital, Tenochtitlan, where they supplied the court, the priesthood, and the army.
options: (A) Empires that funded their governments mainly by monopolizing the long-distance luxury trade while leaving conquered peoples untaxed.
(B) Societies that replaced all taxation with voluntary religious donations.
(C) States whose assemblies of commoners voted each year on how much tribute to pay.
(D) Expanding empires that financed the state, its priests, and its armies by extracting goods and labor from conquered peoples.
explanation: The passage shows conquered provinces paying regular tribute in goods that sustained the Aztec court, religion, and military. This matches the wider pattern of tributary empires — Inca, Roman, Ottoman — whose power rested on systematic extraction from subject peoples.

stem: Which of the following interpretations of the mit'a system is best supported by the passage?
stimulus: In the Inca Empire, households owed the state rotating labor called mit'a: men built terraces, roads, and storehouses, mined, or served in the army for set periods, then returned to their villages. The state, in turn, distributed food, cloth, and chicha beer at festivals and in times of famine, presenting the emperor as a generous provider.
options: (A) The mit'a was a labor obligation that bound households to the state, pairing state demands with reciprocal distributions that legitimated Inca rule.
(B) The mit'a was a form of voluntary wage labor that free households could choose to join or leave at will, much like workers taking jobs in a modern market economy.
(C) The mit'a was a system of chattel slavery in which workers were owned as private property.
(D) The mit'a freed households from every other duty they owed to the Inca state.
explanation: The passage describes a two-way relationship: households owed rotating labor, and the state redistributed goods in return. This reciprocal obligation was central to how the Inca state mobilized labor and justified its authority over subject communities.

stem: Which statement about the spread of Islam in West Africa is best supported by the passage?
stimulus: In 1324 Mansa Musa, ruler of Mali, crossed the Sahara to Mecca on the hajj with a caravan carrying vast quantities of gold. On his return he built mosques and brought Muslim scholars to Mali. Decades later, the traveler Ibn Battuta found the people of Mali eager to memorize the Quran, while griots still recited the deeds of pre-Islamic kings at court.
options: (A) Islam spread through Mali mainly by military campaigns of forced conversion that wiped out older beliefs and replaced them with Islamic law.
(B) Malian rulers rejected Islam entirely in order to preserve traditional religion.
(C) Trans-Saharan trade and royal patronage carried Islam into Mali's elite and urban culture, while older customs continued alongside it.
(D) West Africa had become fully Islamic long before any trans-Saharan trade existed.
explanation: Mansa Musa's hajj and mosque-building show elite patronage, and Ibn Battuta's account shows Quranic learning at court alongside griots honoring pre-Islamic kings. Islam arrived through trade contacts and royal adoption, blending with rather than erasing local traditions.

stem: Ibn Battuta's observations in the excerpt most directly reflect which of the following about his historical situation?
stimulus: Shared stimulus for items 001-003. Adapted from Ibn Battuta's account of his visit to the Mali Empire around 1352: 'The people are eager to memorize the Quran. Yet I was shocked when the sultan's female cousins entered unveiled, for such mixing is forbidden by our law.'
options: (A) He traveled as a Moroccan envoy to convert West Africans to Islam.
(B) He judged the societies he visited by the standards of Islamic law and scholarship.
(C) He wrote to entertain European readers with exotic African tales.
(D) He traveled as a merchant chasing profits in the gold trade.
explanation: Ibn Battuta was a trained Muslim jurist, and the Rihla is his account of the wider Islamic world. His praise for Quranic learning and his shock at unveiled royal women show him measuring Mali against the legal and scholarly norms he carried from Morocco — what he notices and how he judges it are shaped by that identity.

stem: Which of the following arguments about Islam in Mali is best supported by the excerpt?

(D) Malian rulers blended Islamic practices with long-standing local customs.
explanation: The passage shows both sides at once: the sultan enforces Friday prayer and rewards Quranic learning, yet griots still sing the old royal praises at court and royal women appear unveiled despite Battuta's disapproval. That combination supports the argument that Mali's elite adopted Islam while keeping established customs, rather than replacing one with the other.

stem: The sultan's ability to reward courtiers with gold, as described in the excerpt, is best understood in which broader context?
stimulus: Shared stimulus for items 001-003. Adapted from Ibn Battuta's account of his visit to the Mali Empire around 1352: 'The people are eager to memorize the Quran. explanation: Mali sat atop the West African goldfields, and camel caravans carried that gold north across the Sahara to North African and Middle Eastern markets — famously illustrated by Mansa Musa's lavish spending on his 1324 pilgrimage. The sultan's gold rewards were possible because Mali controlled one end of this lucrative trans-Saharan trade.

stem: Polo's description most strongly suggests that he wrote for an audience that would be impressed by which of the following?

explanation: Polo dwells on bridges, crowded markets, goods from every province, and universal paper money — the marvels of a commercial economy. As a Venetian merchant writing for Europeans, he highlights exactly what would astonish them: the size and organization of Chinese trade.

stem: Which of the following best explains the commercial development described in the excerpt?

explanation: Hangzhou's commercial boom began under the Song dynasty, whose cities, market networks, and paper money made China the world's most commercialized economy. The Mongols preserved and extended that system — keeping paper currency and the Grand Canal — which is why Polo found such a thriving market city under the Yuan.

stem: A historian claims that Yuan China had the most monetized economy in the world at the time. Which evidence from the excerpt best supports that claim?

(B) Pepper and ginger arriving from every province
(C) Hangzhou's large population living by trade and crafts in its many crowded market quarters
(D) Even small everyday purchases being paid for with the government's paper money
explanation: A monetized economy is one where money is used widely in daily transactions. Polo's note that even small purchases were made with state paper money shows currency reaching ordinary buyers and sellers — direct evidence of deep monetization, which bridges, imports, or occupations alone do not prove.

stem: Which of the following comparisons between the overland routes shown on the map is best supported?
stimulus: Shared stimulus for items 007-010. Map titled 'Silk Road Trade (c. 1200 CE).' explanation: The map labels each good at its point of origin: finished luxuries like silk, porcelain, and tea flow out of China, while horses, furs, and incense originate in the interior and West Asia. The roads carried value in both directions, not just one way.

stem: The expansion of the exchange networks shown on the map is best understood in the broader context of which development?

stem: A historian argues that the Mongol Empire was primarily a destructive force with little positive historical significance. Which of the following best evaluates that interpretation using the map?
stimulus: Shared stimulus for items 007-010. Map titled 'Silk Road Trade (c. 1200 CE).' Dashed red lines mark overland caravan routes running from Chang'an (Xi'an) through Samarkand, Merv, and Baghdad to Constantinople and the Black Sea ports, with a southern branch passing through India. options: (A) The interpretation is fully correct, because trade routes bypassed all Mongol lands.
(B) The interpretation is fully correct, because no cities at all existed anywhere within Mongol territory and the steppe produced nothing of value worth trading with anyone.
(C) The interpretation is partly right, because sea routes mattered more than land routes.

explanation: The conquests were brutally destructive, but the map shows the Silk Roads running straight through Mongol-held Central Asia around 1200-1300, busy with labeled goods. That pattern fits the Pax Mongolica: Mongol guards, relay stations, and merchant partnerships made the land routes safer than before, so calling the empire only destructive misses a major part of the story.

stem: A historian claims that Mongol rule created conditions that encouraged long-distance exchange. Which evidence from the map best supports that claim?

A red line marks the route of Marco Polo (1271-1295), running overland from Europe across the empire to China and back by sea.
options: (A) Marco Polo's marked route crosses several khanates, showing one traveler could journey from Europe to China under Mongol protection.
(B) Each khanate developed a wholly separate language and religion.
(C) The Yuan court refused to accept any tribute from the other khanates.
(D) The Golden Horde blocked all trade between Europe and Asia.
explanation: Marco Polo's route is marked running from Europe across the whole Mongol realm to China, and the map shows all four khanates as parts of one empire. Safe passage across that system is exactly the condition that let merchants, envoys, and missionaries travel farther than before.

stem: The position of Yuan China shown on the map is best understood in which broader context?

(B) The Yuan rulers completely rejected every Chinese administrative tradition and governed China purely as steppe nomads with no bureaucracy at all.
(C) Yuan China was the wealthiest and most populous of the khanates, at the heart of the Mongol system.
(D) The Yuan was a minor state overshadowed by the Golden Horde.
explanation: The map shows the EMPIRE OF THE GREAT KHAN (Yuan) as the largest of the four divisions, and Marco Polo's marked route ends at its court in China. Khubilai Khan's court drew Persian astronomers, Central Asian administrators, and European visitors - the map's pattern reflects a China at the center of, and plugged into, a continent-wide Mongol system.

stem: Which of the following best explains the political development shown on the map — the division of the Mongol Empire into four khanates?
stimulus: Shared stimulus for items 011-013. Map titled 'Asia under the Mongols, 1290 A.D.' A red line marks the route of Marco Polo (1271-1295), running overland from Europe across the empire to China and back by sea.
options: (A) The Mongols gave up their empire because nomadic life could not work with ruling cities.

(C) European crusaders conquered the western empire and split it among themselves.
(D) The khanates divided because a single Mongol defeat in the attempted invasions of Japan destroyed all Mongol military power.
explanation: Chinggis Khan's empire was simply too large for one court to govern, and Mongol succession customs produced rival claimants after each khan's death. By 1279 the result was four khanates under his descendants — still linked by trade and tribute, as the arrows show, but ruling themselves.

stem: The pattern shown on the map best supports which of the following connections between trade and disease?

(C) Land routes spread the plague, but the sea routes were left completely untouched.
(D) The same networks that moved silk, spices, and paper also moved pathogens, so commercial integration exposed the whole region to pandemic.
explanation: The plague's dated advance follows the trade corridors: from the Black Sea ports and the Levant by ship to Constantinople, Alexandria, and Italy, then inland and onward across Europe. The map makes the connection visible - the commercial integration that enriched the region also gave a pathogen a continent-wide highway.

stem: A historian claims that the plague caused major economic disruption across Afro-Eurasia. Which of the following would be the best evidence to support that claim?

options: (A) Records of steep population losses followed by rising wages and greater peasant mobility in many regions
(B) Proof that the trade routes were abandoned forever after 1353 and never used again
(C) Documents showing the plague struck only Europe and spared Asia and the Middle East
(D) Tax registers demonstrating that government revenues climbed steadily through the worst plague years because rulers taxed the survivors more heavily
explanation: When a third or more of the population dies, workers become scarce and their labor becomes valuable — so wages rose and peasants could move or bargain for better terms in many regions. Population collapse followed by labor-market upheaval is exactly the economic fingerprint of the plague.

stem: Two historians debate the plague's significance. One calls it 'a European catastrophe'; the other calls it 'a Eurasian turning point.' Which argument is best supported by the map?

(C) The second historian, because the map shows the plague sweeping from the Levant and Crimea across all of Europe, Russia, and North Africa - far beyond a single region

stem: The purpose of the edict is best understood as which of the following?
stimulus: Shared stimulus for items 017-018. Adapted from a Yuan dynasty edict on paper currency: 'The Great Khan has ordered that paper notes, stamped with the imperial seal, shall be the lawful money of the realm. Merchants must accept them in all markets from Khanbaliq to the ports. Whoever counterfeits the notes or refuses them shall be punished severely, for the notes carry the empire's guarantee.'
options: (A) To persuade merchants to give up long-distance trade and return to farming
(B) To assert state control over the money supply and force acceptance of imperial notes
(C) To invite foreign merchants to set up their own private mints and coinage inside China
(D) To preserve a folk tale about the invention of paper as entertainment
explanation: The edict commands acceptance of the Khan's notes in every market and threatens severe punishment for refusal or counterfeiting. Its purpose is political and economic at once: to make the state's paper the realm's single currency and to back it with imperial authority.

stem: A historian claims that China had the world's most advanced credit and money economy in this period. Which of the following, combined with the edict, would best support that claim?

(B) The continued use of cowrie shells as the sole currency in Chinese markets
(C) The total absence of merchants from the cities of Yuan China
(D) Merchants' use of bills of exchange and deposit banking alongside state paper money
explanation: The edict shows state paper money; bills of exchange and deposit banking show merchants moving large sums without carrying coin or notes — the credit side of a sophisticated money economy. Together they show both government currency and private financial instruments at work, which is what 'most advanced' requires.

stem: Which of the following best explains how Kilwa developed into a wealthy city-state?
stimulus: Shared stimulus for items 019-020. A description of Kilwa, on the Swahili coast, around 1330: 'The sultan mints copper coins stamped in Arabic. The Great Mosque, built of coral stone, overlooks the harbor where dhows unload cloth and porcelain from Cambay and Arabia. In exchange, merchants carry away gold brought from the interior, where great stone-walled towns command the trade.'
options: (A) It acted as a middleman, trading Indian Ocean cloth and porcelain for African interior gold.
(B) It seized the interior goldfields with a powerful standing army and forced miners to work for the sultan.
(C) It taxed European ships sailing through the Strait of Malacca.
(D) It quit trade after adopting Islam and lived by farming alone.
explanation: Kilwa produced neither the cloth nor the gold — its wealth came from sitting between them. Dhows brought Asian manufactures to its harbor, and caravans brought gold from interior towns like Great Zimbabwe; Kilwa's merchants profited on the exchange at both ends, the classic middleman position.

stem: Kilwa's Islamization and Arabic coinage are best understood in which broader context?
stimulus: Shared stimulus for items 019-020. A description of Kilwa, on the Swahili coast, around 1330: 'The sultan mints copper coins stamped in Arabic. (B) The complete isolation of sub-Saharan Africa from Indian Ocean commerce
(C) The spread of Islam along Indian Ocean trade routes through steady merchant contact rather than conquest
(D) The rejection of all foreign cultural influences by Swahili rulers
explanation: On the Swahili coast no conquering army arrived; instead, generations of Arab and Persian merchants married locally, built mosques, and traded, and coastal rulers adopted Islam as they joined that commercial world. Arabic-script coins and a coral-stone mosque are the marks of a faith carried by commerce, not by invasion.

stem: The wind patterns shown best explain which of the following features of Indian Ocean trade?
stimulus: Shared stimulus for items 021-022. Monsoon and trade-wind chart of the Indian Ocean (U.S. Navy, 1859), showing prevailing winds in February (left) and August (right). In February the winds blow from the northeast, carrying ships from India toward Arabia and Africa; in August they reverse to the southwest, carrying ships back toward India.
options: (A) Merchants sailed the same routes in both directions and completed round trips within a single month
(B) Voyages followed the seasons, so ports filled with merchants waiting for the winds to turn.
(C) Ships avoided the Indian Ocean and used only overland routes.
(D) Monsoon winds kept dhows from ever reaching East Africa.
explanation: Because the winds reverse with the seasons, a sailor could only go one way at a time and had to wait months for the return wind. That rhythm shaped the whole trading world: ports like Calicut and Aden swelled with merchants and goods each season as everyone waited for the winds to turn.

stem: A historian claims that mastery of the monsoon system made the Indian Ocean the most reliable long-distance trade network of the period. Which evidence would best support that claim?
stimulus: Shared stimulus for items 021-022. Monsoon and trade-wind chart of the Indian Ocean (U.S. Navy, 1859), showing prevailing winds in February (left) and August (right). In February the winds blow from the northeast, carrying ships from India toward Arabia and Africa; in August they reverse to the southwest, carrying ships back toward India.
options: (A) Monsoon winds blew so unpredictably from season to season that they sank most of the ships that ever attempted the crossing, making scheduled trade impossible.
(B) Indian Ocean merchants moved their goods entirely by camel caravan.
(C) No ship crossed the Indian Ocean before the year 1500.
(D) Sailors built large dhows with lateen sails to catch the seasonal winds, and entrepot ports grew busy on sailing-season schedules.
explanation: Reliability came from predictability: the monsoons reversed on schedule every year, so sailors could plan voyages around them. Purpose-built ships like lateen-rigged dhows and ports organized around the sailing calendar show a whole commercial system engineered around that dependable rhythm — exactly what would make the network the most reliable of its age.

stem: The handbook entry most directly reflects which of the following about its author's historical situation?
stimulus: Adapted from Francesco Pegolotti's merchant handbook, c. 1340: 'The road from Tana to Cathay is perfectly safe, whether by day or by night. A merchant with proper papers will find organized relay stations with food and lodging every day's journey. You may travel with a woman and gold and fear nothing.'
options: (A) He wrote practical guidance for European merchants traveling under Mongol protection.
(B) He was a Mongol official ordering merchants to pay higher taxes.
(C) He wrote a religious text urging Christians to shun Asia.
(D) He was a Chinese scholar-official writing to criticize the presence of foreign merchants in Yuan China.
explanation: The author gives nuts-and-bolts travel advice — papers, relay stations, safety — aimed at merchants like himself heading to 'Cathay' (China). The relay stations are the Mongol yam system, and the boasted safety is the Pax Mongolica; the passage is a European merchant's practical guide to a Mongol-secured route.

stem: Which of the following arguments about West African states is best supported by the excerpt?
stimulus: A description of trans-Saharan trade, c. 1300: 'Salt from the desert mines is cut into slabs and carried south by camel caravan. In the Sahel markets, one slab buys gold dust weighed on small scales. The kings of Mali tax every load that enters and leaves their lands, and with this revenue they maintain armies, mosques, and the city of Timbuktu.'
options: (A) Mali's rulers enriched themselves by marching north and conquering the desert salt mines outright.
(B) The gold-salt trade mattered little economically next to local farming.
(C) Taxing trade routes gave Sahelian rulers the revenue to build states, armies, and cities.
(D) Trans-Saharan trade enriched North Africa while impoverishing West Africa.
explanation: The passage connects the dots directly: Mali's kings taxed every caravan load, and that tax revenue paid for armies, mosques, and Timbuktu itself. The argument that trade taxation funded state-building is the one the evidence actually traces — revenue in, institutions out.

stem: A historian claims that the diffusion of champa rice transformed Chinese society. Which evidence from the account best supports that claim?
stimulus: A Song dynasty account notes: 'Champa rice, brought from the southern kingdom of Champa, ripens early and resists drought. In the Yangzi valley, farmers now harvest two crops a year where one grew before. The registers record twice as many households as a century ago.'
options: (A) The rice originally came from the kingdom of Champa.
(B) Farmers could double-crop, and the registered population greatly increased.
(C) The account was written during the Song dynasty.
(D) Before champa rice arrived, Yangzi valley farmers had been limited to a single annual crop.
explanation: 'Transformed society' needs evidence of deep change, and the account supplies it: two harvests a year meant far more food, and the doubled household registers show the population surge that followed. Origin, date, and the old single crop describe background — the double harvest and population growth are the transformation.

stem: Which of the following best explains the process by which gunpowder technology spread across Eurasia?
stimulus: A historian's summary of weapons technology: 'Gunpowder was invented in China, where Song armies used fire-lances and bombs. Mongol conquerors carried the knowledge westward; by the 1300s, metal-barreled cannon appeared in the Middle East and Europe, where rulers quickly adopted them for siege warfare.'
options: (A) European inventors created gunpowder on their own and exported it to China.
(B) Chinese merchants guarded the secret so well that it never left East Asia.
(C) The technology spread westward solely through peaceful scholarly exchanges at medieval universities, where professors shared formulas with visiting students.
(D) Mongol conquests carried Chinese military knowledge west, where other societies adapted it to their own siege warfare.
explanation: The summary traces a clear sequence: invention in Song China, westward transmission by the Mongols, then local adoption — Middle Eastern and European rulers casting their own cannon for their own sieges. Conquest moved the knowledge; receiving societies then adapted the technology rather than merely copying it.

stem: The spread of Islam described here is best understood in which broader context?
stimulus: An account of Sumatra in the 1300s: 'In the port of Samudera, the ruler has embraced Islam. Sufi teachers from Arabia and India preach in the markets, and local chiefs who trade with them take Muslim names. No armies came; the faith arrived with the monsoon ships.'
options: (A) Islam moved along Indian Ocean trade routes mainly through merchants and Sufi teachers, not armies.
(B) The Mongol Empire forcibly converted all of Southeast Asia to Islam.
(C) Southeast Asian rulers adopted Islam chiefly to win military aid from the distant Abbasid caliphate.
(D) Islam reached Southeast Asia only after Europeans arrived in the 1500s.
explanation: The account stresses that 'no armies came' — conversion followed commerce. Sufi preachers and traders carried the faith on the monsoon routes, and port rulers adopted it as they joined the Muslim trading world. That pattern — trade-borne, not conquest-borne, Islam — is the broader context for Southeast Asia.

stem: Which of the following comparisons between Venice and Kilwa is best supported by the description?
stimulus: Two trading city-states, c. 1300: Venice, at the head of the Adriatic, grew rich carrying Eastern spices and silks into Europe in its galleys, and its merchants financed voyages with sea-loans. Kilwa, on the Swahili coast, grew rich carrying Arabian cloth and Indian porcelain into Africa in its dhows, exchanging them for interior gold.
options: (A) Both cities depended chiefly on overland camel caravans crossing the deserts and steppes of the interior, rather than on any ships at all, for their prosperity.
(B) Venice used its navy to dominate and control Kilwa's commerce.
(C) Both thrived as middlemen linking producers and buyers across regions, with ships and credit fitted to their own seas.
(D) Kilwa grew rich by manufacturing goods while Venice lived by farming alone.
explanation: Neither city made what it sold: Venice moved Eastern goods into Europe, Kilwa moved Asian goods into Africa for gold — both profiting as go-betweens. Each used the tools of its own waters, galleys and sea-loans in the Mediterranean, dhows in the Indian Ocean, to do the same middleman work.

stem: Which of the following arguments about the plague's consequences is best supported by the accounts?
stimulus: Adapted from accounts of the plague's aftermath: 'In England, so many laborers died that surviving workers demanded triple wages, and lords who once bound peasants to the land now competed to hire them. In the Egyptian countryside, the loss of farmers shrank the harvests, and the Mamluk treasury, starved of taxes, debased its coinage.'
options: (A) The plague increased the power of landlords and governments in every region that it struck, since the survivors had no choice but to obey.
(B) Huge death tolls gave surviving workers more bargaining power in some places while draining state treasuries in others.
(C) The plague caused no serious economic harm anywhere outside England.
(D) Governments easily replaced lost taxes by minting more valuable coins.
explanation: The two cases point in different directions, and the best argument respects both: in England, scarcity of labor let workers demand higher wages from competing lords, while in Egypt the same mortality shrank harvests and tax revenue, forcing the Mamluks to debase their coins. One catastrophe, but its economic effects depended on local conditions.

stem: The panel best reflects which of the following about its makers' historical situation?
stimulus: Illuminated panel from the Catalan Atlas, made in Majorca in 1375: a dark-skinned crowned king sits on a throne holding a large gold nugget in one hand and a scepter in the other. A caption reads: 'This Black lord is called Musa Mali, lord of the Black people of Guinea. So abundant is the gold found in his country that he is the richest and most noble king in all the land.'
options: (A) Majorcan mapmakers had sailed to Mali themselves and interviewed Mansa Musa.
(B) Europeans in the 1300s knew nothing of West Africa and pictured it as empty land.
(C) The Mali Empire itself commissioned the atlas in order to celebrate its own immense wealth.
(D) Europeans learned of West African wealth through trans-Saharan trade reports, which the mapmakers used to portray a famed African king.
explanation: The mapmakers never visited Mali — Mansa Musa had died decades before 1375 — yet they knew exactly what made him famous: gold. That knowledge traveled north with the trans-Saharan caravans and the tales of Musa's 1324 pilgrimage, reaching Mediterranean mapmakers who turned secondhand reports into this golden portrait.

stem: The production of documents such as the one shown most directly reflects which of the following about the Ottoman state in the sixteenth century?
stimulus: Image: a 16th-century Ottoman imperial ferman (decree), opening with the sultan's illuminated tughra, his imperial monogram, in blue and gold calligraphy. The decree text in Ottoman Turkish follows below, carrying the sultan's orders to his officials.
options: (A) The sultan governed the provinces through religious scholars alone, without any secular officials.

(D) Lawmaking authority had been handed down to janissary garrisons in the provinces.
explanation: The kanunname combined the sultan's own regulations with Islamic law and was issued to provincial officials, showing a central state imposing uniform rules. Suleyman earned the title 'Lawgiver' for exactly this systematizing work.

stem: A historian claims that imperial decrees such as the one shown strengthened the sultan's authority by presenting him as both an Islamic ruler and a sovereign lawgiver in his own right. Which feature of the document best supports this claim?
stimulus: Image: a 16th-century Ottoman imperial ferman (decree), opening with the sultan's illuminated tughra, his imperial monogram, in blue and gold calligraphy. The decree text in Ottoman Turkish follows below, carrying the sultan's orders to his officials.
options: (A) The text pairs references to Islamic law with the sultan's own kanun regulations issued under his tughra.
(B) The tughra proves that Suleyman personally wrote out every copy of the code by hand in the palace scriptorium.
(C) The ornate decoration shows that the laws were meant only for display inside the palace.
(D) The criminal penalties listed prove that Islamic courts were abolished under Suleyman.
explanation: Pairing sharia with the sultan's own legislation under his personal monogram is exactly the dual image the claim describes: guardian of Islam and independent lawgiver.

stem: The intended audience for the decree shown was most likely:

options: (A) European ambassadors negotiating commercial privileges and capitulation treaties with the Ottoman Porte.
